voice_attribution_risks.note: Parenthesis inserted by Engels (fn12, 4th German edition) sits inside Marx's text and could read as Marx's own.
Opens with 'Some people might think...' (opponent's view) before Marx's answer; easy to misread.
Footnote 16 has Adam Smith's view, then Marx's assessment, then Engels's bracketed note on Work vs Labour.
Footnote 21 quotes Broadhurst at length then mocks him; Engels's bracketed note ends it.
Satirical portrait of mercantilists and free-trade 'bagmen'; irony that could be taken as a claim.
Footnote 26 mixes Proudhon's ideal, Marx's joke about popes and Catholics, and Goethe; reader must track each voice.
Footnote 26a is an editors' (MECW) note from the German edition, not Marx.
Footnote 34 quotes Marx's own 1847 book, and footnotes 32-33 argue with Ricardo's text as quoted.
Block quote of an economist's view; Marx's reply follows in the commodities' voice.
Many quoted authors (Locke, Law, Galiani) presented in sequence; some are opponents, others support.
Economists' view ('discoverers of this chemical element') is presented as theirs; Marx's answer is in the same paragraph.
A gentleman's view that building brings poor is quoted; Marx's answer comes in later paragraphs.
Lord Dufferin's proposal is quoted, and the German 'Wie menschlich' is ironic, not Marx's approval.
A defender of enclosures is quoted against Dr. Price; the reader must not take his view as Marx's.
Eden's 'stoical peace of mind' is Marx's framing of Eden's conclusion, which is ironic.
A Tory's quote on wages is introduced as 'naïve'; Marx's ironic comment follows.
Mirabeau's praise of discrete workshops is quoted; footnote 4 explains Mirabeau's view as a product of its time.
Gülich's praise of Holland is quoted, then corrected by Marx in the same paragraph.
Wakefield's 'social contract' is quoted; the mockery belongs to Marx, not to Wakefield.
Molinari's footnote is quoted in French, followed by Marx's sarcastic 'How generous Mr. Molinari!'.
Condillac's long quoted passage opens with 'It is not true'; a reader may miss that Marx rejects it.
Torrens's 'Effectual demand' is quoted in the body text; Marx's answer follows, so keep the quote and the rebuttal clearly split.
Two propositions, 'Capital is money' and 'Capital is commodities', come from Mercantilist and Mill sources, then Marx says value is the active factor.
'inwardly circumcised Jews' is Marx's satirical image of the capitalist's view of commodities; the wording is a sharp, antisemitic-tinged image that a rewriter must handle deliberately.
The 'Eden of the innate rights of man' passage is ironic; a reader could take Freedom/Equality/Property/Bentham as Marx's approval.
Storch's 'risks nothing' and the bakers' report are quoted inside footnotes; keep the attribution clear.
Adam Smith's quoted passage on the money quantity is partly praised, partly rejected by Marx; a reader may take it as Marx's own view.
MacCulloch is praised for an 'anticipation' in the footnote; Marx's irony sits inside the quote; keep the mockery visible.
the capitalist's excuses and his 'practical man' rebuttal are voiced in narration; the irony must not be read as Marx's view
Voltaire's Pangloss line is set as Marx's irony about the capitalist's gain, with the translation in brackets
'gift of Nature which costs the labourer nothing' is Marx's ironic description of the capitalist's view, not a claim that labour is free
a critic of Ricardo's 'Obs.' is quoted and then mocked as a wiseacre; Marx's judgement sits in the same paragraph
'Mr. Carey and other harmonisers' is Marx's irony; the 18% rate is the apologists' figure

dialogue with Senior in second person; 'you' is the professor, not the reader
James Wilson's 'last hour' cry is attributed to him, but its tone is Marx's
the worker's long speech is unquoted; attributing it to Marx would misrepresent the argument
